bottom_line: In patients hospitalized for an acute coronary syndrome within the preceding 10 days, 80 mg of atorvastatin daily vs 40 mg of pravastatin daily reduced the primary end point at two years (22.4% vs 26.3%), with a 16% hazard reduction (95% confidence interval, 5 to 26 percent).
implications: These data support that, in this trial population, high-dose atorvastatin produced a lower 2-year Kaplan–Meier primary end-point rate than standard-dose pravastatin (22.4% vs 26.3%) and was associated with more frequent ALT elevations >3× ULN (3.3% vs 1.1%). The results do not establish the mechanism of benefit or whether differences are due solely to LDL lowering, and they were obtained in a "carefully selected and monitored study population."

major_points.text: Randomized comparison of standard-dose pravastatin vs high-dose atorvastatin after recent acute coronary syndrome.
major_points.quote: We enrolled 4162 patients who had been hospitalized for an acute coronary syndrome within the preceding 10 days and compared 40 mg of pravastatin daily (standard therapy) with 80 mg of atorvastatin daily (intensive therapy).

major_points.text: Primary end point was a composite including death, MI, unstable angina rehospitalization, late revascularization, and stroke.
major_points.quote: The primary end point was a composite of death from any cause, myocardial infarction, documented unstable angina requiring rehospitalization, revascularization (performed at least 30 days after randomization), and stroke.

major_points.text: Achieved median LDL differed substantially between arms during treatment.
major_points.quote: The median LDL cholesterol level achieved during treatment was 95 mg per deciliter (2.46 mmol per liter) in the standard-dose pravastatin group and 62 mg per deciliter (1.60 mmol per liter) in the high-dose atorvastatin group (P<0.001).

major_points.text: Primary end point at two years was lower with atorvastatin, and the prespecified equivalence criterion was not met.
major_points.quote: Kaplan–Meier estimates of the rates of the primary end point at two years were 26.3 percent in the pravastatin group and 22.4 percent in the atorvastatin group, reflecting a 16 percent reduction in the hazard ratio in favor of atorvastatin (P=0.005; 95 percent confidence interval, 5 to 26 percent).

major_points.text: ALT elevations >3× ULN occurred more often with high-dose atorvastatin.
major_points.quote: The percentages of patients who had elevations in alanine aminotransferase levels that were more than three times the upper limit of normal were 1.1 percent in the pravastatin group and 3.3 percent in the atorvastatin group (P<0.001).

major_points.text: No rhabdomyolysis was reported in either group.
major_points.quote: There were no cases of rhabdomyolysis in either group.

absolute_effects.text: Kaplan–Meier estimates of the primary end point at two years: 26.3% (pravastatin) vs 22.4% (atorvastatin).
absolute_effects.quote: Kaplan–Meier event rates of the primary end point at two years were 26.3 percent in the standard-dose pravastatin group and 22.4 percent in the high-dose atorva- statin group

absolute_effects.text: 2-year event rates for death from any cause: 2.2% (atorvastatin) vs 3.2% (pravastatin).

absolute_effects.quote: more than three times the upper limit of normal were 1.1 percent in the pravastatin group and 3.3 percent in the atorvastatin group (P<0.001).

subgroups.text: Benefit was consistent across prespecified subgroups including sex, index presentation, and diabetes status.
subgroups.quote: The benefit of high-dose atorvastatin was con- sistent across the prespecified subgroups, including men and women, patients with unstable angina and those with myocardial infarction, and those with and those without diabetes mellitus

subgroups.text: Interaction was significant only for baseline LDL ≥125 mg/dl vs <125 mg/dl (P=0.02).
subgroups.quote: A test for interaction was significant only for a base-line low-density lipoprotein (LDL) value of at least 125 mg per deci- liter, as compared with a value of less than 125 mg per deciliter (P=0.02).

subgroups.text: Greater hazard reduction in baseline LDL ≥125 mg/dl subgroup than <125 mg/dl.
subgroups.quote: a base-line LDL cholesterol level of at least 125 mg per deciliter, a prespecified subgroup, with a 34 per- cent reduction in the hazard ratio, as compared with a 7 percent reduction

harms.text: Discontinuation rates at one year and two years were reported and did not differ significantly.
harms.quote: The rates of discontinuation of treatment because of an adverse event or the patient’s preference or for other reasons were 21.4 percent in the pravastatin group and 22.8 percent in the atorvastatin group at one year

harms.text: ALT >3× ULN was more common with atorvastatin.
harms.quote: elevations in alanine aminotransferase lev- els that were more than three times the upper limit of normal were 1.1 percent in the pravastatin group and 3.3 percent in the atorvastatin group (P<0.001).

harms.text: Study medication discontinued by investigators for myalgias/muscle aches or CK elevations in 2.7% vs 3.3%.
harms.quote: discontinued by the in- vestigators because of a report of myalgias or mus- cle aches or elevations in creatine kinase levels in 2.7 percent of pravastatin-treated patients, as com- pared with 3.3 percent of atorvastatin-treated pa- tients

harms.text: No rhabdomyolysis occurred in either group.
harms.quote: There were no cases of rhabdomy- olysis in either group.
